stem: What would be the electron dot structure of carbon dioxide which has the formula CO₂?
solution:
Carbon has **four** valence electrons and each oxygen has **six**. Carbon needs four more and each oxygen needs two more, so carbon forms a **double bond with each oxygen** — two shared pairs on either side.

Writing \(\times\) for carbon's electrons and \(\bullet\) for oxygen's, the structure is

**O :: C :: O**

- Between the left oxygen and carbon: **two shared pairs** (four electrons).
- Between carbon and the right oxygen: **two shared pairs** (four electrons).
- Each oxygen also carries **two lone pairs** of its own.

Counting round each atom: carbon has 8 electrons (its own 4 plus 4 shared in), and each oxygen has 8 (its own 6 plus 2 shared in). Every atom has a completed octet. In line notation this is \(\text{O} = \text{C} = \text{O}\).
groundedIn: §4.1 Bonding in Carbon — the Covalent Bond, which builds the double bond in oxygen (Fig. 4.3) and the triple bond in nitrogen (Fig. 4.4) from exactly this counting, and states that carbon completes its octet by sharing its four valence electrons.

stem: What would be the electron dot structure of a molecule of sulphur which is made up of eight atoms of sulphur? (Hint — The eight atoms of sulphur are joined together in the form of a ring.)
solution:
Sulphur has **six** valence electrons, so each atom needs **two** more to complete its octet. In a ring of eight atoms every sulphur is bonded to **two neighbours**, and one shared pair with each neighbour supplies exactly the two electrons it needs.

So \(\text{S}_8\) is a **ring of eight sulphur atoms joined by eight single covalent bonds**:

- Each S–S bond is **one shared pair** (a single bond).
- Each sulphur also keeps **two lone pairs** of its own.

Counting round any atom: 4 electrons in its two lone pairs, plus 2 shared pairs = 8. The octet is complete on all eight atoms, and there are no double bonds anywhere in the ring.
groundedIn: §4.1 Bonding in Carbon — the Covalent Bond, which defines a single covalent bond as one shared pair (Figs. 4.1 and 4.2) and works the octet count for molecules of hydrogen, chlorine, oxygen and nitrogen the same way.

stem: How many structural isomers can you draw for pentane?
solution:
**Three.**

Pentane is \(\text{C}_5\text{H}_{12}\), and the three isomers differ only in how the five carbon atoms are arranged:

1. **n-Pentane** — all five carbons in one straight chain:

\(\text{CH}_3 - \text{CH}_2 - \text{CH}_2 - \text{CH}_2 - \text{CH}_3\)

2. **Iso-pentane** — a four-carbon chain with a \(\text{CH}_3\) branch on the second carbon.

3. **Neo-pentane** — a three-carbon chain with **two** \(\text{CH}_3\) branches on the middle carbon, giving a central carbon bonded to four \(\text{CH}_3\) groups.

All three have the same molecular formula but different structures, which is what makes them structural isomers. A fourth arrangement cannot be drawn — any attempt simply redraws one of these three.
groundedIn: §4.2.2 Chains, Branches and Rings, which introduces straight chains, branched chains and rings and defines compounds with the same formula but different structures as structural isomers.

stem: What are the two properties of carbon which lead to the huge number of carbon compounds we see around us?
solution:
**1. Catenation.** Carbon has the unique ability to **form bonds with other carbon atoms**, giving long chains, branched chains and rings, with the carbons joined by single, double or triple bonds. No other element shows catenation to anything like this extent — silicon manages chains of only seven or eight atoms, and those are very reactive. The carbon–carbon bond is very strong and therefore stable.

**2. Tetravalency.** Carbon has a **valency of four**, so one carbon atom can bond to four other atoms — of carbon, or of hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen, sulphur, chlorine and many others. Each different partner gives a compound with its own properties.

Together these two properties produce compounds numbering in the **millions**, more than all the other elements put together.
groundedIn: §4.2 Versatile Nature of Carbon, which names catenation and tetravalency as the two factors and gives the silicon comparison and the millions figure.

stem: What will be the formula and electron dot structure of cyclopentane?
solution:
**Formula: \(\text{C}_5\text{H}_{10}\).**

Cyclopentane is a **ring of five carbon atoms**. Each carbon uses two of its four bonds to join its two neighbours in the ring, which leaves **two bonds free on each carbon** — so each carries two hydrogen atoms: \(5 \times \text{CH}_2 = \text{C}_5\text{H}_{10}\).

**Electron dot structure.** Draw the five carbons in a pentagon. Then:

- Between each neighbouring pair of carbons, **one shared pair** of electrons (a single C–C bond) — five such bonds round the ring.
- On each carbon, **two shared pairs with two hydrogen atoms**, one pair per hydrogen.

Every carbon then has four shared pairs, so its octet is complete, and every hydrogen has one shared pair, completing its K shell.
groundedIn: §4.2.2 Chains, Branches and Rings, which shows cyclohexane and cyclopentane as carbon rings (Fig. 4.7), with §4.1 for the shared-pair counting.

context: Draw the structures for the following compounds.
solution:
**Ethanoic acid** — *eth-* means two carbons, *-oic acid* means the carboxyl group \(-\text{COOH}\).

\(\text{CH}_3 - \text{COOH}\)

Drawn out: the first carbon carries three hydrogens; the second is double-bonded to one oxygen and single-bonded to an \(-\text{OH}\) group.
groundedIn: §4.2.5 Nomenclature of Carbon Compounds with Table 4.4, which gives the prefix and suffix for each class — -ol for alcohol, -al for aldehyde, -one for ketone, -oic acid for carboxylic acid, chloro-/bromo- for halo alkanes — and §4.2.4 Homologous Series for the carbon count in the stem name.

context: Draw the structures for the following compounds.
solution:
**Bromopentane** — *pent-* means five carbons, *bromo-* is a bromine atom replacing one hydrogen.

\(\text{CH}_3 - \text{CH}_2 - \text{CH}_2 - \text{CH}_2 - \text{CH}_2\text{Br}\)

**Are structural isomers possible for bromopentane?** **Yes — three**, because the bromine can sit on the first, second or third carbon of the chain:

- **1-bromopentane**: \(\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{Br}\)
- **2-bromopentane**: \(\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CHBrCH}_3\)
- **3-bromopentane**: \(\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CHBrCH}_2\text{CH}_3\)

Positions 4 and 5 are not new — turning the chain end for end makes them the same as 2 and 1.
groundedIn: §4.2.5 Nomenclature of Carbon Compounds with Table 4.4, which gives the prefix and suffix for each class — -ol for alcohol, -al for aldehyde, -one for ketone, -oic acid for carboxylic acid, chloro-/bromo- for halo alkanes — and §4.2.4 Homologous Series for the carbon count in the stem name.

context: Draw the structures for the following compounds.
solution:
**Butanone** — *but-* means four carbons, *-one* means the ketone group \(\text{C} = \text{O}\) on a carbon inside the chain.

\(\text{CH}_3 - \text{CO} - \text{CH}_2 - \text{CH}_3\)

The carbonyl group must be on the **second** carbon: a \(\text{C} = \text{O}\) at the end of the chain would be an aldehyde, not a ketone.
groundedIn: §4.2.5 Nomenclature of Carbon Compounds with Table 4.4, which gives the prefix and suffix for each class — -ol for alcohol, -al for aldehyde, -one for ketone, -oic acid for carboxylic acid, chloro-/bromo- for halo alkanes — and §4.2.4 Homologous Series for the carbon count in the stem name.

context: Draw the structures for the following compounds.
solution:
**Hexanal** — *hex-* means six carbons, *-al* means the aldehyde group \(-\text{CHO}\), which always sits at the **end** of the chain.

\(\text{CH}_3 - \text{CH}_2 - \text{CH}_2 - \text{CH}_2 - \text{CH}_2 - \text{CHO}\)
groundedIn: §4.2.5 Nomenclature of Carbon Compounds with Table 4.4, which gives the prefix and suffix for each class — -ol for alcohol, -al for aldehyde, -one for ketone, -oic acid for carboxylic acid, chloro-/bromo- for halo alkanes — and §4.2.4 Homologous Series for the carbon count in the stem name.

context: How would you name the following compounds?
solution:
**Bromoethane.**

Two carbons in the chain give the stem *eth-*, and the bromine atom is named with the prefix *bromo-*.
groundedIn: §4.2.5 Nomenclature of Carbon Compounds with Table 4.4, which gives the prefix and suffix for each class — -ol for alcohol, -al for aldehyde, -one for ketone, -oic acid for carboxylic acid, chloro-/bromo- for halo alkanes — and §4.2.4 Homologous Series for the carbon count in the stem name.

context: How would you name the following compounds?
stem: A compound in which a carbon atom carries two hydrogen atoms and is double-bonded to an oxygen atom — printed as H—CHO.
solution:
**Methanal** (commonly called formaldehyde).

\(\text{HCHO}\)

There is only **one** carbon, so the stem is *meth-*; the \(-\text{CHO}\) group at the end of the chain is an aldehyde, which takes the suffix *-al*.
groundedIn: §4.2.5 Nomenclature of Carbon Compounds with Table 4.4, which gives the prefix and suffix for each class — -ol for alcohol, -al for aldehyde, -one for ketone, -oic acid for carboxylic acid, chloro-/bromo- for halo alkanes — and §4.2.4 Homologous Series for the carbon count in the stem name.

context: How would you name the following compounds?
stem: A six-carbon chain carrying a triple bond between the last two carbon atoms — printed as \(\text{CH}_3 - \text{CH}_2 - \text{CH}_2 - \text{CH}_2 - \text{C} \equiv \text{CH}\).
solution:
**Hexyne** (more fully, **hex-1-yne**).

- Six carbon atoms in the chain give the stem *hex-*.
- A **triple bond** between carbon atoms makes it an alkyne, which takes the suffix *-yne*.

Counting the carbons from the end nearer the triple bond puts it at position 1, so the full name is hex-1-yne. The compound is **unsaturated**.
groundedIn: §4.2.5 Nomenclature of Carbon Compounds with Table 4.4, which gives the prefix and suffix for each class — -ol for alcohol, -al for aldehyde, -one for ketone, -oic acid for carboxylic acid, chloro-/bromo- for halo alkanes — and §4.2.4 Homologous Series for the carbon count in the stem name.

stem: Why is the conversion of ethanol to ethanoic acid an oxidation reaction?
solution:
Because **oxygen is added** to the ethanol.

\(\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{OH} \xrightarrow{\text{alkaline } \text{KMnO}_4} \text{CH}_3\text{COOH}\)

Compare the two formulae: ethanol is \(\text{C}_2\text{H}_6\text{O}\) and ethanoic acid is \(\text{C}_2\text{H}_4\text{O}_2\). The molecule has **gained one oxygen atom and lost two hydrogen atoms** — both of which are oxidation.

The reagents used, alkaline potassium permanganate or acidified potassium dichromate, are the ones supplying that oxygen, which is exactly why they are called **oxidising agents**.
groundedIn: §4.3.2 Oxidation with Activity 4.5, where alcohols are converted to carboxylic acids by alkaline potassium permanganate, described as adding oxygen to the starting material.

stem: A mixture of oxygen and ethyne is burnt for welding. Can you tell why a mixture of ethyne and air is not used?
solution:
Welding needs a **very hot flame**, and that requires ethyne to burn **completely**.

- **Ethyne burnt in pure oxygen** gets all the oxygen it needs, so combustion is complete and the flame is clean, blue and extremely hot — hot enough to melt metal.
- **Ethyne burnt in air** has only about a fifth as much oxygen available, so combustion is **incomplete**. Ethyne is an **unsaturated** hydrocarbon, and an unsaturated compound burning in a limited supply of air gives a **yellow, sooty flame** with a great deal of black smoke, at a much lower temperature.

A sooty, cooler flame would neither melt the metal nor leave a clean joint, so pure oxygen is used.
groundedIn: §4.3.1 Combustion with Activities 4.3 and 4.4, which record that saturated hydrocarbons give a clean flame while unsaturated ones give a yellow sooty flame, and that limiting the air supply causes incomplete combustion.

stem: How would you distinguish experimentally between an alcohol and a carboxylic acid?
solution:
Use a test that only the **acid** can pass. Two work:

**1. Sodium hydrogencarbonate test (the clearest).** Add a pinch of sodium hydrogencarbonate to each sample.

- The **carboxylic acid** gives **brisk effervescence** — carbon dioxide, which turns lime water milky:

\(\text{CH}_3\text{COOH} + \text{NaHCO}_3 \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{COONa} + \text{H}_2\text{O} + \text{CO}_2\)

- The **alcohol** gives no reaction at all.

**2. Litmus test.** A carboxylic acid turns **blue litmus red**; an alcohol leaves litmus unchanged, being neutral.

The first test is the better one, because the gas is visible and can itself be confirmed with lime water.
groundedIn: §4.4.2 Properties of Ethanoic Acid with Activity 4.7 and Activity 4.9 — the litmus and pH comparison, and the reaction with carbonates and hydrogencarbonates giving a salt, carbon dioxide and water.

**Oxidising agents are substances capable of adding oxygen to others.**

In this chapter the examples are **alkaline potassium permanganate** and **acidified potassium dichromate**. Each converts an alcohol into a carboxylic acid — that is, it adds oxygen to the starting material — which is why it earns the name.
groundedIn: §4.3.2 Oxidation, which states that substances capable of adding oxygen to others are known as oxidising agents and names alkaline potassium permanganate and acidified potassium dichromate.

stem: Would you be able to check if water is hard by using a detergent?
solution:
**No.**

The test for hard water works because **soap** reacts with the calcium and magnesium salts that make water hard, forming an insoluble **scum** and giving very little foam. Soft water gives plenty of foam and no scum, so the difference is easy to see.

**Detergents behave the same way in both kinds of water.** Their charged ends **do not form insoluble precipitates** with calcium and magnesium ions, so a detergent lathers well and leaves no scum whether the water is hard or soft — and that is precisely why detergents are used in hard water.

With no difference to observe, a detergent cannot tell you whether water is hard. Use soap for the test.
groundedIn: §4.5 Soaps and Detergents with Activities 4.11 and 4.12, which compare foam and curdy precipitate in hard and soft water, and the closing paragraph stating that detergents do not form insoluble precipitates with calcium and magnesium ions.

stem: People use a variety of methods to wash clothes. Usually after adding the soap, they ‘beat’ the clothes on a stone, or beat it with a paddle, scrub with a brush or the mixture is agitated in a washing machine. Why is agitation necessary to get clean clothes?
solution:
Soap does two separate jobs, and only the first happens on its own.

**What the soap does by itself.** Most dirt is oily. The soap molecule has a hydrophobic hydrocarbon tail that goes into the oil and an ionic head that stays in the water, so the molecules surround each oil droplet and form a **micelle**, holding the dirt suspended.

**What agitation does.** The dirt is stuck to the fibres of the cloth. Beating, scrubbing or agitating supplies the **mechanical energy needed to loosen the oily dirt from the fibres** so that the micelles can carry it away, and it helps the micelles disperse into the water rather than settle back.

Without agitation the soap would form micelles around dirt it has never managed to lift off the cloth, and the clothes would not come clean.
groundedIn: §4.5 Soaps and Detergents with Fig. 4.13 and Activity 4.10 — the micelle, the hydrophobic tail in the oil droplet and the ionic end facing the water, and the emulsion that pulls the dirt out into the water.
